en.title: Committed Use, Cache Rates, and the Mid-Year True-Up
en.titleCore: Committed use, cache rates and true-ups
en.description: At procurement scale the bill is set by the floor, the cache rate and the pass-through clause. Four contract terms that decide more spend than model choice does.
en.body:
AI model spend has moved from a line item to a procurement category. At that scale the mechanics that govern a large bill are not the same ones that govern a small one, and the negotiation is almost never about the headline rate.

Term 1: the floor, and who owns the risk

A committed-use agreement typically trades 10–35% off list for a 12-month floor. That is a bet on your own forecast, and the failure mode is specific: commit to a floor, then optimise onto a cheaper model, and end up paying committed rates for tokens you no longer need. Three controls make the bet survivable.

  • Size the floor to steady demand only. Batch, evals and internal traffic forecast far better than customer-facing agent traffic.
  • Keep model selection fungible. A commitment to spend with a provider is portable across that provider's models. A commitment to a named model is not, and it is the term to refuse.
  • Review at month six, not twelve. If run-rate is far under the floor, renegotiate before the true-up, not after.

Term 2: the cache rate

Cached input is billed as a separate rate and, on cache-heavy agent workloads, is the majority of input cost. Reported flagship rates put cache reads at $0.20 per million against $4.00 for fresh input. Negotiate the cache rate explicitly — it is a separate line in the rate card and a separate line on the invoice.

Term 3: the line items the rate card missed

Server-side tools are billed independently of tokens. Web search, code execution and similar server tools produce a non-token cost that no headline rate negotiation touched, and on an agent built around web search it can be substantial. Ask for the tool-unit rates and the monthly tool ceiling, separately from the token commitment.

Term 4: the pass-through clause

This is the clause that matters most. When two labs cut prices on the same afternoon, a rate card locked six months earlier becomes the expensive option. Structure the agreement so provider price revisions pass through, or trigger a review window. Without it, every price cut by a competitor raises your cost until renewal.

Bottom line

Committed floor, cache rate, tool ceiling, pass-through clause. Those four terms decide more of the bill than which model you chose, and they are the terms to negotiate before the renewal date, not after.

faq.question: How should we size a committed-use floor for AI spend?
faq.answer: Base it on steady, forecastable demand such as batch, evals and internal traffic rather than customer-facing agent traffic. Keep model selection fungible across the term, and renegotiate at month six if run-rate is materially under the floor.

faq.question: Why negotiate the cached-input rate separately?
faq.answer: Cache reads are a separate rate card line and, on cache-heavy agent workloads, the majority of input cost. Reported flagship rates put cache reads around $0.20 per million against $4.00 for fresh input, so the cache rate drives the invoice.

faq.question: Which contract clause matters most for AI spend?
faq.answer: The pass-through or price-review clause. When competitors cut prices mid-term, a locked rate card becomes the expensive option until renewal. Without a pass-through or review trigger, external price cuts raise your cost.

faq.question: What do server-side tools cost on a large AI agreement?
faq.answer: They are billed independently of tokens, so no headline rate negotiation covers them. On an agent built around server-side web search or code execution the tool cost can be substantial, so ask for tool-unit rates and a monthly ceiling separately.
